items.title: US Department of Labor proposes to update fiduciary rule to affirm Employee Retirement Income Security Act’s exclusive purpose rule
items.content_text: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Employee Benefits Security Administration today issued proposed amendments to the investment duties regulation to clarify the fiduciary duty of loyalty under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act.The proposed rule seeks to end the 32-year uncertainty surrounding whether ERISA allows fiduciaries to consider non-financial factors in retirement plan investments, including environmental, social, and governance, and diversity, equity, and inclusion. The proposal gives fiduciaries an affirmative expression of their duty of loyalty, which would clarify that ERISA requires plan fiduciaries to act solely in the interest of the plan’s participants and beneficiaries, and for the exclusive purpose of providing for the interests of participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan.“President Trump’s Department of Labor is not putting its thumb on the scale for or against any particular investment or asset class,” said U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “Our proposed rule makes clear that retirement plan fiduciaries must make investment decisions solely in the financial interests of workers and retirees, not to advance political or social agendas. items.content_html: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Employee Benefits Security Administration today issued proposed amendments to the investment duties regulation to clarify the fiduciary duty of loyalty under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act.The proposed rule seeks to end the 32-year uncertainty surrounding whether ERISA allows fiduciaries to consider non-financial factors in retirement plan investments, including environmental, social, and governance, and diversity, equity, and inclusion. The proposal gives fiduciaries an affirmative expression of their duty of loyalty, which would clarify that ERISA requires plan fiduciaries to act solely in the interest of the plan’s participants and beneficiaries, and for the exclusive purpose of providing for the interests of participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan.“President Trump’s Department of Labor is not putting its thumb on the scale for or against any particular investment or asset class,” said U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “Our proposed rule makes clear that retirement plan fiduciaries must make investment decisions solely in the financial interests of workers and retirees, not to advance political or social agendas. Our focus is on protecting and growing Americans’ retirement savings, which have reached record levels thanks to President Trump.”If finalized, the proposal would also place a heightened focus on shareholder engagement and proxy voting by fiduciaries to secure the retirement interests of American workers and would avoid the improper pressures and influence placed on plan fiduciaries. This includes voting shares and otherwise attempting to influence corporate behavior through shareholder engagement activities for ESG/DEI purposes. The proposed rule follows the directive in President Trump’s executive order, “Protecting American Investors from Foreign-Owned and Politically Motivated Proxy Advisors,” which instructed the department to strengthen the fiduciary standards of pension and retirement plans covered by ERISA.“President Trump has directed the department to assess whether certain proxy advisor firms spreading ESG and DEI are acting solely in the financial interest of plan participants,” said Assistant Secretary for the Employee Benefits Security Administration Daniel Aronowitz. “Our proposed rule does just that by making clear what is, and what isn’t, loyal behavior when it comes to proxy voting and shareholder engagement.” The proposal would remove two departmental inventions that are not consistent with ERISA and may be misused by fiduciaries with ulterior motives – the tiebreaker test and the participant preference provision. Under the tiebreaker test, a fiduciary can say that two investments are “equal” and then pick their preferred investment, which may include ESG funds. Similarly, fiduciaries can elicit the views of participants who support ESG investments and use that as a pretext to permit investments they otherwise would not be allowed to include under federal retirement laws. The proposed rule will be published in the Nov. 24 edition of the Federal Register, with public comments due 60 days after its publication.EBSA ensures the security of retirement, health, and other job-based benefits for American workers and their families. The agency is responsible for protecting more than 155 million workers, retirees, and their families, who are covered by approximately 2.8 million health plans, 837,000 private retirement plans, and 521,000 additional welfare benefit plans. Together, these plans hold about $15.2 trillion in assets.Employers and workers can contact EBSA at askebsa.dol.gov or call 866-444-3272 toll-free for help with private sector job-based retirement and health plans.Read the notice of proposed rulemaking on Loyalty and the Exclusive Purpose Rule in Selecting Plan Investments and Exercising Shareholder Rights.

items.title: US Department of Labor announces final rule clarifying employee, independent contractor status under federal wage and hour laws
items.content_text: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division today announced a final rule to revise its analysis for distinguishing between employees and independent contractors under the Fair Labor Standards Act and two related federal laws. items.content_html: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor’s Wage and Hour Division today announced a final rule to revise its analysis for distinguishing between employees and independent contractors under the Fair Labor Standards Act and two related federal laws. The new final rule provides clarity to businesses and workers alike, as well as the division’s enforcement personnel.U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling, Wage and Hour Division Administrator Andrew Rogers, and other department officials hosted an event to formally announce the final rule at the Frances Perkins Building this morning. Employers, business associations, worker advocates, independent contractors, and other stakeholders were in attendance as Secretary Sonderling highlighted the clarity and simplicity of the new regulations.The final rule rescinds an earlier 2024 rule addressing the classification of employees and independent contractors and replaces it with an analysis that is substantially similar to the framework adopted by the department in 2021. Consistent with the outcomes of federal appellate cases, the final rule provides further guidance on the process for differentiating between employees with protections under the FLSA and individuals who work as independent contractors.“It’s more important than ever to ensure our labor regulations keep pace with the changing ways that Americans choose to work, and businesses choose to operate,” said Secretary Sonderling. “The new Independent Contractor final rule establishes clear, predictable, and easy-to-understand criteria for determining who is an employee and who is an independent contractor – allowing millions of Americans to take advantage of new opportunities in President Trump’s booming economy.”The final rule also applies the department’s streamlined analysis to the Family and Medical Leave Act, and the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act, both of which use the FLSA’s statutory definition of “employ.” However, the rule does not change the assessment of employee or independent contractor status for the purpose of any other federal laws, including the Internal Revenue Code, and does not preempt any state or local laws.“The Department of Labor is committed to helping employers prevent misclassification. This rule strikes the right balance by protecting employees who are entitled to the protections of federal wage and hour laws, while also respecting the entrepreneurial spirit of legitimate independent contractors,” said Administrator Rogers. “The department distilled longstanding judicial tests into a framework that employees and employers can reliably apply at the outset of business relationships.”The analysis in the department’s final rule does the following:Applies an “economic reality” test to determine whether a worker is in business for himself or herself as an independent contractor or is an employee economically dependent on an employer for work.Identifies and explains two “core factors” to help determine if a worker is economically dependent on an employer for work or in business for himself or herself:The nature and degree of control over the work.The worker’s opportunity for profit or loss based on initiative and/or investment.Identifies other factors to help determine a worker’s status as an employee or independent contractor, including the amount of skill required for the work, the degree of permanence of the working relationship, and whether the work is part of an integrated unit of production.Advises that the actual practice of the worker and the potential employer is more relevant than what may be contractually or theoretically possible.Provides 14 fact-specific examples applying the factors to real-life circumstances. The department published a notice of proposed rulemaking on Feb. 27, 2026, and received approximately 16,500 public comments during a 60-day comment period. After reviewing this feedback, the department finalized the rule with modifications and enhancements. For example, in response to commenter requests, the final rule includes new illustrative examples involving farm labor contractors, digital platform workers, and truck drivers.Workers and employers can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the FMLA.WATCH the Independent Contractor Final Rule Announcement.Read Secretary Sonderling’s Op-Ed on the Final Rule.Read the final rule, which takes effect 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

items.title: US Department of Labor obtains court order requiring NJ-based  construction contractor to pay $2.2M in back wages, damages, penalties
items.content_text: ENGLEWOOD CLIFFS, NJ – The U.S. Department of Labor has obtained a consent judgment requiring a construction contractor to pay more than $2 million in back wages and damages to 323 construction workers.     Entered Nov. 16, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, the consent judgment resolves the department’s litigation alleging Premier Concrete Systems LLC and its owners, Peter Tiflinsky and Antonio Escada, violated overtime and recordkeeping provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act.The litigation was a result of an investigation by the department’s Wage and Hour Division that found the company and its owners paid employees cash at straight-time rates for all hours worked and failed to pay them time and one-half their regular rate of pay for hours over 40 in a workweek as required by the FLSA. “Construction workers play a critical role across the country in ensuring safe and reliable structures. The Wage and Hour Division is committed to ensuring that construction workers are paid in compliance with federal labor laws,” said Wage and Hour Division Regional Administrator James Cain in Philadelphia.The judgment requires Premier Concrete Systems to pay 323 employees back wages totaling $1,040,648 and an equal amount in damages. The judgment also requires the defendants to pay a civil penalty of $118,704 and prohibits defendants from violating the FLSA in the future.“The resolution of this case is a clear reminder for employers in the construction industry to remember their responsibilities under the law,” said Regional Solicitor of Labor Jeffrey S. items.title: US Department of Labor cites powder coating company for willful toxic substance exposures, repeat violations, proposes more than $1.6M in penalties
items.content_text: HOUSTON – The U.S. Department of Labor has cited a powder coating and furniture restoration company for willfully and repeatedly exposing workers to toxic substances and other safety and health hazards.The department’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration conducted three inspections of Outdoor Furniture Refinishing Inc. – doing business as Allied Powder Coating – on April 10, 2026. One inspection addressed complaint items after the employer provided an inadequate response to an inquiry, and two follow-up inspections were initiated in relation to safety and health violations found during a December 2023 inspection. The employer’s failure to submit abatement documentation prompted a comprehensive review of ongoing hazards.OSHA cited the company for three willful violations for exposing workers to hazardous levels of 1,3,5-triglycidyl isocyanurate and total dust during powder coating operations. The agency also issued 18 serious violations for failing to provide training on excessive noise exposure and for deficiencies involving respiratory protection, hazard communication, personal protective equipment, forklift operations, electrical safety, and portable ladders.In addition, OSHA cited the company for 18 repeat violations related to respiratory protection, noise overexposure, spray booths, hazard communication, compressed air, and electrical hazards. The agency also issued one other-than-serious violation for unsanitary working conditions.OSHA has proposed $1,640,888 in penalties.The agency found that, despite multiple inspections since 2013 and a formal settlement agreement finalized in December 2024, the company has failed to take meaningful action to correct recurring violations.The employer has 15 business days from receipt of its citations and penalties to comply, request an informal conference with OSHA’s area director, or contest the findings before the independent Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission. items.title: US Labor Department cites New Jersey pastry maker, staffing agency for endangering workers after 2 injuries in 3 months; proposes $351K in fines
items.content_text: PEDRICKTOWN, NJ – The U.S. Department of Labor has cited a pastry manufacturer and a staffing agency for endangering employees by exposing them to hazardous energy and amputation hazards.Investigators with the Occupational Safety and Health Administration responded to an April 28 incident at Banneton Bakery LLC and found that an employee provided to the bakery by Idalia’s Staffing Agency was cleaning a moving conveyor belt when their arm got stuck, requiring medical treatment.During the investigation into the April 2026 incident, OSHA learned of a similar event that occurred on Jan. 16, 2026, in which an employee was cleaning the same conveyor belt and suffered a broken arm because the machinery was not locked out during the cleaning.The agency cited Banneton for two willful violations for failing to develop and use lockout/tagout procedures and failing to provide adequate training to ensure employees understood the purpose and function of energy control programs. The bakery also received citations for three serious violations for neglecting to ensure side rails of a ladder extended at least 42 inches above the top access level, not protecting workers from falling through a ladderway floor hole, and not using group lockout devices properly.In addition, OSHA cited Idalia’s Staffing Agency with a serious violation for not ensuring temporary employees received training on using lockout/tagout procedures.The agency proposed $340,479 in penalties for Banneton Bakery and $10,641 in penalties for Idalia’s Staffing Agency.The employers have 15 business days from receipt of the citations and penalties to comply, request an informal conference with OSHA’s area director, or contest the findings before the independent Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission. Please check the OSHA establishment search page periodically for any changes in the inspection or penalty status.Visit OSHA’s website to learn about controlling hazardous energy. items.title: Fisheries of the Northeastern United States; Atlantic Bluefish Fishery; Quota Transfer From Rhode Island to North Carolina
items.content_text: NMFS announces that the State of Rhode Island is transferring a portion of their 2026 commercial bluefish quota to the State of North Carolina. This quota adjustment is necessary to comply with the Atlantic Bluefish Fishery Management Plan (FMP) quota transfer provisions. This announcement informs the public of the revised 2026 commercial bluefish quotas for Rhode Island and North Carolina.

items.title: Standing Order: Standing Order Requiring Paper Filing for Election Day 2026 Emergency Matters
items.content_text:
STATE OF MAINE       SUPERIOR COURT 
DISTRICT COURT 
 
  
STANDING ORDER REQUIRING 
PAPER FILING FOR ELECTION DAY 
2026 EMERGENCY MATTERS 
 
 
 The Maine Judicial Branch (MJB) is implementing the Maine eCourts 
system – including eFiling – statewide.1  EFileMaine is a practical and efficient 
document submission system already in use in many courts throughout the 
state.  However, because filings related to Election Day may be uniquely time-
sensitive, to ensure timely processing, the MJB will require paper filing under 
the limited circumstances described below.   
 
 It is therefore ORDERED that any emergency Title 21-A filings related to 
Election Day 2026 filed between 4:00 p.m. on Friday, October 30, 2026, and 
9:00 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, must be by paper, unless otherwise 
ordered.2 
 
It is further ORDERED that the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems 
are SUSPENDED to the extent necessary to give effect to this order.   
 
 
 
Dated: 10/28/2026   _____/s/______________________   
       Chief Justice Robert E. Mullen 
 
 
 
Dated: 10/28/2026   ___/s/_______________________   
       Chief Judge Brent Davis 
 
1 Further information about the Maine eCourts system is available at 
https://www.courts.maine.gov/ecourts/index.html 
2 Any Election Day 2026 filings filed by eFile during this period may not be processed until the next business 
day after the election.

items.title: Jennifer L. Owen v. Town and Country Federal Credit Union
items.content_text:
MAINE SUPREME JUDICIAL COURT      Reporter of Decisions 
Decision:  2026 ME 105 
Docket:   BCD-23-442 
Argued:   September 11, 2024 
Decided:  November 3, 2026 
 
Panel:  STANFILL, C.J., and MEAD, LAWRENCE, DOUGLAS, JJ., and HUMPHREY, A.R.J. 
 
 
JENNIFER L. OWEN 
 
v. 
 
TOWN AND COUNTRY FEDERAL CREDIT UNION 
 
DOUGLAS, J. 
[¶1]  Jennifer L. Owen appeals from a judgment entered in the Business 
and Consumer Docket (Duddy, J.) after a jury trial in favor of Town and Country 
Federal Credit Union on her claims alleging disability discrimination and 
retaliation.  Owen contends that the court abused its discretion by (1) ordering 
her to pay attorney fees and costs as a discovery sanction, and (2) excluding 
evidence of other former employees’ discrimination claims against Town and 
Country.  We affirm the judgment. 
 2 
I.  BACKGROUND 
A. Owen’s Employment by Town and Country 
[¶2]  The following facts are drawn from competent evidence admitted 
at trial, viewed in the light most favorable to the jury’s verdict in favor of Town 
and Country.  See Sullivan v. Porter, 2004 ME 134, ¶ 12, 861 A.2d 625.   
[¶3]  Town and Country hired Owen as a teller in 2012.  The following 
year, Owen was diagnosed with breast cancer.  Owen remained employed with 
Town and Country and received support from her employer during her 
treatment and recovery.  Town and Country and its employees organized a bake 
sale, a yard sale, and other events to raise money to help her pay her medical 
expenses.  Town and Country allowed other employees to donate paid time off 
to Owen during her treatment.  By early 2014, Owen was cancer-free.

manager in one of Town and Country’s South Portland branches.  In this 
position, Owen was entrusted with managerial responsibilities in addition to 
working with members on loans.

items.title: US Department of Labor recovers $603K for 829 workers  denied overtime pay by Indiana auto parts manufacturer
items.content_text: INDIANAPOLIS – The U.S. Department of Labor has recovered $603,953 in back wages for 829 workers after an investigation found an Indianapolis-area vehicle parts manufacturer failed to properly calculate overtime wages.Investigators with the department’s Wage and Hour Division found that Toa (USA) LLC, a major automotive supplier that serves top-tier automotive companies, did not include a non-discretionary attendance bonus for hourly employees when calculating overtime during applicable workweeks, in violation of the overtime provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act. “When employers pay commissions, differentials, certain bonuses, stipends, or other incentives, they must include them in the calculation of overtime pay,” said Wage and Hour Division District Director Juan Herrera in Indianapolis. “We encourage employers, especially those who offer various types of incentive pay, to review our compliance assistance materials and contact us with any questions about overtime requirements.”Toa (USA) LLC, with manufacturing facilities in Mooresville, is the primary body structure and suspension components supplier for Subaru of Indiana Automotive and Toyota Motor Engineering & Manufacturing North America.Employees and employers can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division. The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the Family and Medical Leave Act.Learn more about the Wage and Hour Division, including a search tool that workers can use if they believe they may be owed back wages collected by the division. items.title: US Department of Labor obtains consent order against retirement plan fiduciaries of defunct Chicago law firm for failing to distribute $6.4M in assets
items.content_text: CHICAGO – Following a complaint filed by the U.S. Department of Labor, a defunct Chicago law firm’s retirement plan distributed $6,498,858 in retirement plan assets to 40 employees. The plan’s fiduciaries failed to properly terminate the plan and disburse those funds as required by law.On Aug. 18, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, Eastern Division, entered a consent order resolving the department’s claims against the McCullough, Campbell & Lane LLP, and the firm’s capital partners David L. Joslyn, John W. McCullough, F. Dennis Nelson, and Paul S. Turner. The department alleged that the defendants violated the Employee Retirement Income Security Act by failing to follow a 2019 partnership resolution. The resolution required them to terminate the firm’s retirement plan and distribute the plan’s assets to employees. The defendants have provided proof that plan’s assets were distributed to participants, except for approximately $13,861 in the employer-level plan accounts. The consent order requires the plan’s recordkeeper to distribute those funds to its participants and to terminate the plan. “After their law firm closed, Turner, McCullough, Nelson, and Joslyn failed to provide employees with their promised retirement benefits,” said Employee Benefits Security Administration Regional Director Kelli Hammerl in Chicago. “The Department of Labor helped participants gain access to their retirement savings.” The order permanently bars Turner, McCullough, Nelson, and Joslyn from serving as fiduciaries or service providers for any ERISA-covered employee benefit plan. The plan transferred account balances belonging to plan participants it could not locate to the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation’s Missing Participants Program.Employers can get help complying with the law through EBSA’s correction programs, which includes the Voluntary Fiduciary Correction Program. The VFCP allows plan officials to correct violations and avoid excise taxes

items.title: US Department of Labor awards $250,000 in Brookwood-Sago Grants to promote mine safety, health education
items.content_text: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor today announced the award of $250,000 in Brookwood-Sago grant funding to two organizations to support education and training initiatives that will help identify and prevent unsafe working conditions in and around the nation’s mines.Administered by the department’s Mine Safety and Health Administration, the Brookwood-Sago Mine Safety grant program helps recipients create training materials, conduct mine safety training, and educational programs designed to protect the safety and health of miners. In awarding the grants, MSHA focused on innovative plans for mine safety and pilot programs that may be useful for miners working in a broad range of positions. The grants also put an emphasis on programs and materials targeting workers in smaller mines that train mine operators and miners about MSHA standards, and emergency response training.Established under the Mine Improvement and New Emergency Response Act of 2006, the grant program honors the miners lost at the Jim Walter Resources #5 mine in Brookwood, Alabama, on Sept. 23, 2001, and at the Sago Mine in Buckhannon, West Virginia, on Jan. 2, 2006.The recipients of the 2026 Brookwood-Sago grants are as follows:RecipientCityState/TerritoryAmountSaelua Medical Corporation Pago PagoAmerican Samoa$170,000University of ArizonaTucsonAZ$80,000
